dsa.title: Complexity Analysis and Problem-Solving Method
dsa.description: Learn to measure an algorithm before you write it. You will use Big-O notation for time and space, read constraints to choose an approach, and follow a repeatable method for every problem in the rest of this track.
topics: Reading constraints to pick an approach
A method: clarify, examples, brute force, optimize, test
Testing with edge cases and counter-examples
dsa.challenge: Implement three solutions to the same problem (a quadratic brute force, a sort-based approach and a hash-based approach), measure their runtime for inputs of 10 to 10 million, and plot how each curve matches its predicted complexity.

children.title: Big-O in practice
children.description: Big-O describes how cost grows with input size and ignores constants. It tells you which approach survives large inputs, not which one is faster for ten items.

children.title: Space complexity
children.description: Memory use matters as much as time, especially for recursion depth and auxiliary arrays. Always state both costs.

children.title: Dynamic array growth
children.description: Appending to a dynamic array is occasionally expensive but cheap on average. Amortized analysis explains why append is still O(1).

children.title: When worst case misleads
children.description: A hash table can degrade to O(n) in theory yet is O(1) in practice. Know which guarantee a data structure really gives.

children.title: A repeatable problem-solving process
children.description: Restate the problem, work an example by hand, find a brute force, then improve it. Doing this out loud is what interviewers look for.

children.title: Constraints as hints
children.description: An input limit of 10^5 means O(n log n) is fine and O(n^2) is not. Constraints often point directly to the intended technique.

children.title: Edge cases
children.description: Empty input, a single element, duplicates, negatives and maximum sizes break more solutions than the main case. List them before coding.

children.title: Writing your own tests
children.description: Compare a fast solution against a slow brute force on random small inputs. A disagreement gives you a minimal failing case for free.

dsa.title: Arrays, Strings, Two Pointers, and Sliding Window
dsa.description: Master the most common data structure and the patterns that make it fast. Two pointers, sliding windows and prefix sums turn many quadratic problems into linear ones.
topics: Sliding window: fixed and variable size

resources.label: NeetCode - Arrays and Hashing / Two Pointers

dsa.challenge: Solve ten problems that need these patterns (for example longest substring without repeats, container with most water, subarray sum equals k) and for each write down the pattern, the invariant and the complexity before coding.

children.title: Array costs
children.description: Index access is O(1) but inserting or removing in the middle shifts elements in O(n). Knowing this drives most data structure choices.

children.title: Strings
children.description: Strings are usually immutable, so repeated concatenation in a loop is quadratic. Collect pieces in a list and join once.

children.title: Opposite-end pointers
children.description: On sorted data, one pointer from each end can find pairs or compare symmetric positions in a single pass.

children.title: Fast and slow pointers
children.description: Two pointers moving at different speeds detect cycles and find midpoints without extra memory.

children.title: Fixed-size windows
children.description: Slide a window of size k by adding the new element and removing the old one, so each step costs O(1) instead of O(k).

children.title: Variable-size windows
children.description: Grow the window to satisfy a condition and shrink it while it stays valid. The invariant you maintain is what makes the solution correct.

children.title: Prefix sums
children.description: A prefix sum array answers any range-sum query in O(1) after one O(n) pass. The same idea extends to counts and XOR.

children.title: In-place techniques
children.description: Reuse the input array to avoid extra memory, for example by partitioning or swapping. Be careful not to overwrite values you still need.

dsa.title: Hashing: Maps, Sets, and Frequency Patterns
dsa.description: Learn why hash tables are the most useful structure in practice and how to use them to turn searches into lookups. You will also understand collisions, load factor and what makes a good key.
topics: Hash functions, collisions and load factor
Hash maps and sets in your language
Hashing pitfalls: mutable keys and ordering
dsa.challenge: Implement your own hash map with separate chaining and dynamic resizing, test it against the built-in on random operations, then solve five problems using maps and sets and compare their runtimes with brute-force versions.

children.title: Hash functions and collisions
children.description: A hash function maps a key to a slot. Two keys can share a slot, so tables must handle collisions with chaining or probing.

children.title: Load factor and resizing
children.description: As a table fills, collisions grow. Doubling the table when it passes a load threshold keeps operations O(1) on average.

children.title: Maps and sets
children.description: Use a set for membership and duplicates, a map for counts and lookups. Both are O(1) on average for insertion and search.

children.title: Keys must be hashable
children.description: A mutable object used as a key can change its hash after insertion and become unreachable. Use tuples or strings as keys.

children.title: Frequency counting
children.description: Counting occurrences with a map solves anagram, majority-element and top-k style problems in one pass.

children.title: Complement lookup
children.description: For each element, check whether the value you need is already stored. This turns the two-sum family from O(n^2) into O(n).

children.title: Canonical keys
children.description: Group items by a normalized form, such as a sorted string for anagrams, so equal groups map to the same key.

children.title: Ordered versus unordered
children.description: Hash tables do not keep sorted order. When you need range queries or sorted iteration, use a tree-based structure instead.

dsa.title: Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues
dsa.description: Build the linear structures that underlie recursion, parsing and scheduling. You will learn when a list beats an array, how a stack models nesting, and how queues model fair ordering.
topics: Implementing a queue with stacks and vice versa
dsa.challenge: Implement a doubly linked list, then build an LRU cache from a hash map plus that list so get and put are both O(1), and write tests for eviction order.

children.title: Node-based structures
children.description: A linked list trades random access for O(1) insertion and removal at a known node. Dummy head nodes remove most special cases.

children.title: Reversal and cycle detection
children.description: Reversing in place and Floyd's fast-slow pointer are two techniques that appear again and again.

children.title: Last in, first out
children.description: A stack models anything nested: function calls, undo, matching brackets. Push and pop are both O(1).

children.title: Monotonic stack
children.description: Keeping a stack in sorted order finds the next greater element for every item in O(n) total.

children.title: First in, first out
children.description: Queues process items in arrival order and are the base of breadth-first search and task scheduling.

children.title: Deques and circular buffers
children.description: A double-ended queue supports both ends in O(1), and a circular buffer gives a fixed-size queue without shifting elements.

children.title: LRU cache
children.description: Combine a hash map for lookup with a linked list for recency order. It is the classic proof that you can build one structure from two.

children.title: Queue from stacks
children.description: Two stacks can simulate a queue with amortized O(1) operations, a good test of understanding amortized cost.

dsa.title: Recursion and Backtracking
dsa.description: Think recursively: define a problem in terms of smaller versions of itself. You will use recursion for divide and conquer, then add backtracking to search all possibilities such as permutations and subsets.
topics: Base case, recursive case and the call stack
Recursion versus iteration and stack depth
dsa.challenge: Write a generic backtracking solver with choose, explore and undo steps, use it to generate all subsets, permutations and valid N-Queens boards, and count how much pruning reduces the search.

children.title: Base case and recursive case
children.description: Every recursive function needs a base case that stops and a step that moves toward it. A missing base case causes a stack overflow.

children.title: The call stack
children.description: Each call uses stack memory, so deep recursion can fail. Convert to iteration with an explicit stack when depth could be large.

children.title: Splitting problems
children.description: Split the input, solve the parts and combine the results. Merge sort and binary search are the standard examples.

children.title: Recurrence relations
children.description: A recurrence like T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n describes the cost. The master theorem gives the answer for most divide-and-conquer algorithms.

children.title: Choose, explore, undo
children.description: Backtracking builds a solution step by step, and when a choice fails it undoes it and tries the next. The undo step is what people forget.

children.title: Subsets and permutations
children.description: Subsets have 2^n results and permutations n!. Recognizing the size of the output tells you the algorithm cannot be faster.

children.title: Cutting off bad branches
children.description: Check constraints as early as possible. In N-Queens, rejecting a conflicting square immediately removes huge subtrees.

children.title: Memoization preview
children.description: When a recursive call repeats the same inputs, caching results avoids the repeated work. This leads directly into dynamic programming.

dsa.title: Sorting and Binary Search
dsa.description: Understand how sorting works and use it as a tool. You will implement the main algorithms, learn what stability means, and apply binary search not just to arrays but to any monotonic answer space.
topics: Insertion, merge, quick and heap sort
Comparison sort lower bound and counting sort
dsa.challenge: Implement merge sort, quicksort with a random pivot and counting sort, benchmark them on random, sorted and many-duplicate inputs, then solve three problems with binary search on the answer such as minimum capacity to ship packages in D days.

children.title: Merge sort and quicksort
children.description: Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) and is stable; quicksort is usually faster in memory but needs a good pivot to avoid O(n^2).

children.title: Counting and radix sort
children.description: When keys are small integers, sorting without comparisons reaches O(n). It beats the comparison-sort limit by using the key structure.

children.title: Stability
children.description: A stable sort keeps equal items in their original order, which matters when sorting by several fields in turn.

children.title: Using the built-in sort
children.description: In practice you call the library sort. Knowing its complexity and key function lets you use it correctly and fast.

children.title: The invariant
children.description: Define exactly what the low and high pointers mean and what is guaranteed about the answer. Almost every binary search bug is an invariant bug.

children.title: Lower and upper bound
children.description: Finding the first element greater than or equal to a value solves insertion points, counts and ranges with one routine.

children.title: Binary search on the answer
children.description: If you can test whether a value works and the result is monotonic, you can binary search the value itself instead of an array.

children.title: Sorting as preprocessing
children.description: Many problems become easy after sorting: intervals, closest pairs, duplicates. Check whether the extra O(n log n) is acceptable.

dsa.title: Trees and Binary Search Trees
dsa.description: Work with hierarchical data. You will traverse binary trees recursively and level by level, use binary search trees for ordered data, and see why balance matters.
topics: Depth-first traversals: pre, in and post order
Binary search trees: search, insert, delete
Balanced trees: AVL and red-black ideas
Lowest common ancestor and path problems
dsa.challenge: Implement a binary search tree with insert, search, delete and the three DFS traversals plus level order, then write a function that validates a BST and one that finds the lowest common ancestor, with tests on skewed and balanced trees.

children.title: Depth-first traversals
children.description: Preorder, inorder and postorder differ only in when you process the node. Inorder on a BST yields sorted values.

children.title: Level order with a queue
children.description: A queue processes a tree level by level. It answers questions about depth, width and shortest paths in unweighted trees.

children.title: Returning information upward
children.description: Many tree problems return a value from each subtree, such as height or sum, and combine them at the parent.

children.title: Path and ancestor problems
children.description: Lowest common ancestor, diameter and maximum path sum all follow the same recursive pattern with a different combine step.

children.title: Search, insert and delete
children.description: A BST keeps left smaller and right larger, so search follows one path. Deletion has three cases: leaf, one child, two children.

children.title: Validating a BST
children.description: Checking only parent-child order is not enough; every node must lie within bounds set by all its ancestors.

children.title: Why balance matters
children.description: A BST built from sorted input becomes a linked list with O(n) operations. Self-balancing trees keep height at O(log n).

children.title: Where trees appear in practice
children.description: Databases and file systems use B-trees, and language libraries use red-black trees for ordered maps and sets.

dsa.title: Heaps and Priority Queues
dsa.description: Use heaps to repeatedly get the smallest or largest item quickly. You will build one from an array, then apply it to top-k, merging and scheduling problems.
topics: The heap property and array representation
Two heaps and the running median
dsa.challenge: Implement a binary min-heap with push, pop and heapify, then use it for a streaming median tracker with two heaps and a task scheduler that always runs the highest-priority ready job.

children.title: Heap property
children.description: A heap is a tree stored in an array where each parent is smaller (min-heap) or larger than its children. The root is always the extreme value.

children.title: Sift up and sift down
children.description: Insertion adds at the end and sifts up; removal moves the last item to the root and sifts down. Both take O(log n).

children.title: Heapify in linear time
children.description: Building a heap from n items by sifting down from the middle takes O(n), better than inserting one by one.

children.title: Heap sort
children.description: Repeatedly removing the maximum sorts in place in O(n log n), though it is usually slower than quicksort in practice.

children.title: Top-k problems
children.description: Keep a heap of size k to find the k largest items in O(n log k) without sorting everything.

children.title: Merging sorted streams
children.description: A heap holding the head of each list always yields the next smallest value, merging k lists in O(N log k).

children.title: Two heaps for the median
children.description: A max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half give the running median in O(log n) per insert.

resources.label: LeetCode - Find Median from Data Stream

children.title: Scheduling
children.description: Operating systems and job queues use priority queues to pick the next task. Ties and priority changes need extra care.

dsa.title: Graphs: Representation, BFS, and DFS
dsa.description: Model relationships as graphs and traverse them. You will choose between adjacency lists and matrices, run BFS and DFS, and use them for connectivity, grids and cycle detection.
topics: Vertices, edges, directed and weighted graphs
Breadth-first search and shortest unweighted paths
dsa.challenge: Build a graph class with adjacency lists, implement BFS and DFS iteratively and recursively, then solve a maze shortest-path problem on a grid and count islands, comparing BFS and DFS where both work.

children.title: Adjacency lists and matrices
children.description: Lists use O(V + E) memory and suit sparse graphs; a matrix uses O(V^2) but answers edge queries in O(1). Most real graphs are sparse.

children.title: Building from problem input
children.description: Edge lists, grids and word relationships all become graphs. Converting the input to a graph is often the key insight.

children.title: Level-by-level exploration
children.description: BFS visits nodes in order of distance from the start, so it gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

children.title: Multi-source BFS
children.description: Start the queue with several sources at once to compute the nearest source for every node, as in rotting oranges.

children.title: Recursive and iterative DFS
children.description: DFS follows one path as deep as possible before backing up. An explicit stack avoids recursion limits on large inputs.

children.title: Connected components
children.description: Run DFS from each unvisited node to count components, such as islands in a grid.

children.title: Cycle detection
children.description: In undirected graphs a visited non-parent neighbor means a cycle; in directed graphs track the nodes on the current path.

children.title: Bipartite check
children.description: Two-color the graph during BFS; a conflict means the graph is not bipartite. It models problems about splitting into two groups.

dsa.title: Shortest Paths, Topological Sort, and Union-Find
dsa.description: Solve the graph problems that appear in routing, dependency resolution and clustering. You will learn Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, topological ordering, minimum spanning trees and disjoint sets.
topics: Dijkstra's algorithm with a priority queue
Minimum spanning trees: Kruskal and Prim
Choosing an algorithm from the graph's properties
dsa.challenge: Build a small route planner: load a weighted road graph, find shortest routes with Dijkstra, detect impossible build orders with topological sort, and use union-find with Kruskal to compute a minimum spanning network, testing each against known answers.

children.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
children.description: Dijkstra repeatedly settles the closest unfinished node using a priority queue. It requires non-negative edge weights.

children.title: Bellman-Ford
children.description: Relaxing every edge V-1 times handles negative weights and detects negative cycles, at higher cost than Dijkstra.

children.title: Topological sort
children.description: A directed acyclic graph can be ordered so every edge goes forward. Build systems and course prerequisites use it, and a cycle means no valid order.

children.title: Kahn's algorithm
children.description: Repeatedly remove nodes with no incoming edges. It produces an order and detects cycles in the same pass.

children.title: Union-Find
children.description: Union-find tracks which items belong to the same group, with near-constant time per operation using path compression and union by rank.

children.title: Connectivity queries
children.description: Use union-find to answer 'are these connected' as edges arrive, which is much cheaper than rerunning a search each time.

children.title: Kruskal's algorithm
children.description: Sort edges by weight and add each one that does not create a cycle, using union-find to check.

children.title: Prim's algorithm
children.description: Grow a tree from one node by always adding the cheapest edge leaving it. It suits dense graphs.

dsa.title: Dynamic Programming I: Memoization and Tabulation
dsa.description: Learn the technique that turns exponential recursion into polynomial time. You will define states and transitions, then implement them top-down with memoization and bottom-up with tables.
topics: 1D problems: climbing stairs, house robber, coin change
Recovering the actual solution, not just the value
dsa.challenge: Solve coin change, longest increasing subsequence and house robber three ways each (plain recursion, memoization, tabulation), measure the speedup, then reduce the memory of each table and reconstruct the chosen items.

children.title: Overlapping subproblems
children.description: If a recursive solution recomputes the same inputs many times, caching results can reduce exponential work to polynomial.

children.title: Optimal substructure
children.description: DP works when an optimal answer is built from optimal answers to smaller problems. Verify this before using it.

children.title: State and transition
children.description: Write down exactly what dp[i] means, then express it in terms of earlier states. Most DP failures come from an unclear definition.

children.title: Base cases and order
children.description: Fill the table in an order that guarantees every dependency is ready. The base cases are the smallest states you can answer directly.

children.title: Memoization
children.description: Add a cache to the recursive function keyed by its arguments. It is the easiest way to get a correct DP solution.

children.title: Tabulation and space reduction
children.description: Fill an array iteratively. If each state needs only the previous few, keep just those and cut memory to O(1).

children.title: Climbing stairs and house robber
children.description: Each is a choice at every step that depends on the previous one or two. They are the standard first DP exercises.

children.title: Coin change and LIS
children.description: Coin change counts or minimizes combinations, and longest increasing subsequence builds up from shorter ones, with an O(n log n) improvement.

dsa.title: Dynamic Programming II: Grids, Strings, and Knapsack
dsa.description: Extend DP to two dimensions and to the problem families that appear most: grid paths, string alignment, knapsack and interval problems. You will learn to spot which family a new problem belongs to.
topics: Grid path counting and minimum path sum
Longest common subsequence and edit distance
dsa.challenge: Implement edit distance and longest common subsequence with traceback to print the actual alignment, solve 0/1 knapsack with items reconstructed, and write a short note describing the state and transition for each of five new problems.

children.title: Path counting and minimum cost
children.description: In a grid, each cell's value comes from the cell above and to the left. Obstacles and costs change only the transition.

children.title: Space optimization on grids
children.description: Row-by-row filling lets you keep one row instead of the whole table.

children.title: Longest common subsequence
children.description: Compare prefixes of two strings: if the last characters match, extend the diagonal; otherwise take the best of dropping one.

children.title: Edit distance
children.description: The minimum insertions, deletions and replacements to turn one string into another. It powers spell checking and diff tools.

children.title: 0/1 knapsack
children.description: For each item, choose take or skip while respecting a capacity. Iterate capacity downward to avoid reusing an item.

children.title: Subset sum and partition
children.description: Many problems reduce to knapsack: can some subset reach a target sum? Recognize the disguise.

children.title: Interval DP
children.description: State is a range [i, j] and you try every split point. Matrix chain multiplication and burst balloons are the standard examples.

children.title: Bitmask DP
children.description: When the set of used items is small (up to about 20), a bitmask in the state tracks it. Traveling salesman is the classic case.

dsa.title: Greedy Algorithms, Intervals, and Bit Manipulation
dsa.description: Learn when a locally best choice is globally best, and how to prove it. You will also handle interval scheduling and use bit tricks that make some problems short and fast.
topics: The greedy-choice property and exchange arguments
Interval scheduling, merging and meeting rooms
Jump game and gas station style problems
XOR, masks and counting set bits
dsa.challenge: Solve interval merging, minimum meeting rooms and activity selection with greedy strategies, prove or disprove greedy for a coin system by counterexample, and implement five bit tricks (single number, power of two, count bits, subsets by mask, swap without temp).

children.title: Greedy choice and proof
children.description: A greedy algorithm is correct only if you can argue the local choice never hurts. An exchange argument is the usual proof.

children.title: When greedy fails
children.description: Coin change with arbitrary denominations breaks the greedy choice. Always hunt for a counterexample before trusting a greedy idea.

children.title: Sort then sweep
children.description: Sorting intervals by start or end makes merging, scheduling and overlap checks a single pass.

children.title: Meeting rooms with a heap
children.description: Track end times of active meetings in a min-heap to find the number of rooms needed.

children.title: Jump game and gas station
children.description: Track the furthest reachable position or the running surplus. One pass replaces a search over all paths.

children.title: Huffman coding
children.description: Repeatedly merge the two least frequent symbols with a heap to build an optimal prefix code.

children.title: Bitwise operators
children.description: AND, OR, XOR, shifts and NOT operate on every bit at once. They are the basis of flags, masks and many compact algorithms.

children.title: XOR tricks and masks
children.description: x ^ x is zero, so XOR finds the lone unpaired value. Masks enumerate all subsets of a small set.

dsa.title: Tries, Segment Trees, and Advanced Structures
dsa.description: Add the specialized structures that solve specific problem classes quickly: prefix search, range queries with updates, and amortized sequences. Knowing they exist is half the skill.
topics: Tries for prefix search and autocomplete
Segment trees for range queries and updates
Sparse tables and range minimum queries
Choosing a structure from query types
dsa.challenge: Implement an autocomplete trie, a segment tree supporting range sum with point updates, and a Fenwick tree for the same, then benchmark all three against a naive array on 100,000 queries and note when each wins.

children.title: Prefix trees
children.description: A trie stores strings character by character, so finding all words with a prefix costs time proportional to the prefix, not the dictionary.

children.title: Autocomplete and word search
children.description: Combine a trie with DFS to list completions or prune a board search. It is much faster than testing each word separately.

children.title: KMP
children.description: The prefix function lets KMP skip ahead after a mismatch, finding a pattern in O(n + m) instead of O(nm).

children.title: Rolling hash
children.description: A rolling hash compares substrings in O(1) after preprocessing, the base of Rabin-Karp and many duplicate-detection tricks.

children.title: Segment trees
children.description: A segment tree answers range queries and point updates in O(log n) by storing summaries of ranges in a tree.

children.title: Fenwick trees
children.description: A Fenwick tree is a compact structure for prefix sums with updates. It is shorter to write than a segment tree when it fits.

children.title: Sparse tables
children.description: When data never changes, a sparse table answers range minimum queries in O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing.

children.title: Choosing the structure
children.description: Ask what queries you need and whether data changes. The answer usually picks the structure for you.

dsa.title: Interview Strategy and Pattern Recognition
dsa.description: Combine everything into performance. You will map problems to patterns quickly, communicate your reasoning, handle hints and follow-ups, and build a practice routine that keeps skills sharp.
topics: Pattern recognition across the whole track
Handling hints and recovering from being stuck
dsa.challenge: Run three timed mock interviews with a peer or recording yourself, each on an unseen medium problem. Review each one: how long to the first working idea, what hint you needed, which edge case you missed, and which pattern it was.

children.title: Mapping problems to patterns
children.description: Keywords and constraints point to a pattern: sorted input suggests two pointers or binary search, shortest path suggests BFS, optimal substructure suggests DP.

children.title: Building a pattern notebook
children.description: After each problem, record the pattern, the trick and the mistake. Reviewing this beats solving random new problems.

children.title: Clarify and think aloud
children.description: State assumptions, ask about input size and edge cases, and narrate your approach. Interviewers evaluate reasoning, not only the final code.

children.title: Using hints well
children.description: A hint is information, not failure. Restate it, test it against your example, and adjust.

children.title: Scaling and memory limits
children.description: Be ready to say what changes if the input does not fit in memory or arrives as a stream.

children.title: Testing your own solution
children.description: Walk through your code with a small example and an edge case before saying you are done.

children.title: Mock interviews
children.description: Practicing under time pressure with another person builds the habits that solo practice cannot.

children.title: A sustainable schedule
children.description: A few problems a week, reviewed properly, beats a short burst of grinding. Track patterns, not problem counts.

system-design.title: System Design Foundations and Estimation
system-design.description: Learn how designers think before drawing boxes. You will turn vague requirements into functional and non-functional goals, estimate load and storage with simple math, and use a framework to structure any design discussion.
topics: Latency, throughput, availability and consistency targets
system-design.challenge: For a photo-sharing app, write requirements, estimate daily active users, requests per second, storage per year and bandwidth, then list the three decisions that most depend on those numbers and what you would change if traffic were ten times higher.

children.title: Functional and non-functional goals
children.description: Functional goals say what the system does; non-functional goals say how well, such as latency, availability and consistency. The second kind drives the architecture.

children.title: Service level objectives
children.description: An SLO turns a vague 'fast and reliable' into a measurable target like 99.9% of requests under 200 ms.

children.title: Back-of-envelope math
children.description: Round aggressively and use powers of ten: a day is about 10^5 seconds. Order of magnitude is enough to choose between designs.

resources.label: Latency numbers every programmer should know

children.title: Storage and bandwidth
children.description: Multiply users by actions by size, then by retention. The result tells you whether one machine, one database or a distributed system is needed.

children.title: A design framework
children.description: Clarify requirements, estimate scale, sketch a high-level design, then dive into the hardest components. Following the same steps each time keeps you from missing parts.

children.title: Reading versus writing
children.description: A system that is read a thousand times per write is designed differently from one that is write-heavy. Identify which you have first.

children.title: There are no perfect designs
children.description: Every choice gains something and loses something. Name both sides and tie your choice to the stated requirements.

children.title: Start simple, then scale
children.description: Begin with the simplest design that meets today's needs and describe how it evolves. Over-engineering is a failure too.

system-design.title: Networking, APIs, and Load Balancing
system-design.description: Understand how clients reach services and how traffic is spread across them. You will compare API styles, understand the transport and DNS layers that affect latency, and place load balancers and gateways.
topics: DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP versions
Load balancing algorithms and health checks
system-design.challenge: Design the public API for a ride-hailing service: choose REST or gRPC for each interface, define pagination and idempotency for the booking call, and sketch load balancing and health checks for the booking service, explaining how a failing instance is removed.

children.title: DNS, TCP and TLS
children.description: Each connection pays for name lookup, a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake. Reusing connections and terminating TLS close to users cuts latency.

children.title: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
children.description: Multiplexing and QUIC reduce head-of-line blocking. Newer protocol versions matter most on unreliable mobile networks.

children.title: REST, GraphQL and gRPC
children.description: REST suits public resource APIs, GraphQL lets clients choose fields, and gRPC gives fast typed calls between services. Pick per boundary.

children.title: Idempotency and retries
children.description: Clients retry on failures, so a repeated request must not charge twice. Idempotency keys make writes safe to repeat.

children.title: Pagination and versioning
children.description: Cursor-based pagination stays stable under inserts, and explicit versions let you change an API without breaking clients.

children.title: Rate limits in the API contract
children.description: Tell clients their limits and how to back off, with standard headers and a clear error response.

children.title: Layer 4 versus layer 7
children.description: Layer 4 forwards connections fast; layer 7 understands HTTP and can route by path, header or cookie at higher cost.

children.title: Algorithms and health checks
children.description: Round robin, least connections and consistent hashing suit different workloads. Health checks remove failed servers automatically.

system-design.title: Databases: Choosing, Modeling, and Indexing
system-design.description: Pick the right store for the data and the queries. You will compare relational and NoSQL models, understand how indexes speed up reads and slow down writes, and use transactions correctly.
topics: Document, key-value, wide-column and graph stores
Choosing a database from the access pattern
system-design.challenge: Model an e-commerce order system in a relational schema, write the five hottest queries, add the minimum set of indexes with EXPLAIN output showing they are used, then decide which part, if any, you would move to a different store and justify it.

children.title: Relational modeling
children.description: Normalize to avoid duplicated facts, and denormalize deliberately when read speed demands it. Constraints keep data correct.

children.title: NoSQL families
children.description: Key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores each optimize one access pattern. Choose by the queries you must answer, not by fashion.

children.title: How B-tree indexes work
children.description: A B-tree keeps keys sorted so lookups and range scans touch few pages. Each index also slows writes and uses space.

children.title: LSM trees
children.description: Log-structured storage turns random writes into sequential ones, which suits write-heavy workloads, at the cost of read amplification.

children.title: Reading query plans
children.description: EXPLAIN shows whether the database uses an index or scans the table. Reading plans is the main performance skill for SQL.

children.title: Composite and covering indexes
children.description: Column order in a multi-column index matters, and a covering index can answer a query without touching the table.

children.title: ACID
children.description: Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability describe what a transaction promises. Know which guarantees your database gives by default.

children.title: Isolation levels and anomalies
children.description: Weaker isolation allows dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads. Pick the weakest level that keeps your invariants safe.

system-design.title: Scaling Data: Replication, Partitioning, and Sharding
system-design.description: Learn how a database grows past one machine. You will use replication for availability and read scaling, partition data across nodes, and handle the hard parts: hot keys, rebalancing and cross-shard queries.
system-design.challenge: Design the storage layer for a messaging app with 500 million users: choose the partition key, explain how you would add shards without downtime using consistent hashing, and describe what a user sees during replication lag.

children.title: Leader-follower replication
children.description: Writes go to one leader and stream to followers, which serve reads and take over if the leader fails.

children.title: Replication lag
children.description: Followers can be behind, so a user may not see their own write. Route a user to the leader after writing, or use session guarantees.

children.title: Failover
children.description: Promoting a follower is easy to do wrongly: you can lose writes or end up with two leaders. Automate it carefully and test it.

children.title: Multi-leader and leaderless
children.description: Several writers improve availability and locality but make conflicts possible. Systems like Dynamo resolve them with versions or quorums.

children.title: Range versus hash partitioning
children.description: Range keeps neighbors together and supports scans; hash spreads load evenly. Pick according to your query pattern.

children.title: Consistent hashing
children.description: Place nodes and keys on a ring so adding a node moves only a small fraction of keys, not all of them.

children.title: Hot keys and rebalancing
children.description: One celebrity account can overload a shard. Split hot keys, add salt, and move partitions gradually.

children.title: Cross-shard work
children.description: Queries and transactions across shards are slow and complex. Design the partition key so most operations stay on one shard.

system-design.title: Caching and Content Delivery
system-design.description: Make systems fast and cheap by avoiding repeated work. You will place caches at each layer, choose write and invalidation strategies, handle stampedes, and use a CDN for global delivery.
topics: Cache layers: browser, CDN, application, database
system-design.challenge: Add caching to a read-heavy product catalog: design cache-aside with Redis, set TTLs and an invalidation path on updates, protect against a stampede when a popular key expires, and put static assets and API responses behind a CDN with explicit cache headers.

children.title: Cache-aside
children.description: The application checks the cache first, loads from the database on a miss and stores the result. It is the most common and the simplest to reason about.

children.title: Write-through and write-back
children.description: Write-through updates cache and store together for consistency; write-back batches writes for speed but risks losing data on a crash.

children.title: LRU, LFU and TTL
children.description: Eviction decides what leaves a full cache. TTLs bound staleness, and the right policy depends on how access repeats.

children.title: Sizing a cache
children.description: Hit rate depends on the working set, not total data. Measure hit ratio before adding memory.

children.title: Invalidation
children.description: Updating or deleting a cached value at the right time is famously hard. Short TTLs plus explicit invalidation on writes is the practical answer.

children.title: Stampedes and hot keys
children.description: When a hot key expires, thousands of requests hit the database at once. Locking, request coalescing and jittered TTLs prevent it.

children.title: CDN basics
children.description: A CDN stores copies of content near users. Static assets are the easy win, and cacheable API responses can follow.

children.title: Cache-Control headers
children.description: Headers like max-age, s-maxage and stale-while-revalidate tell browsers and CDNs how long to keep a response.

system-design.title: Asynchronous Processing: Queues, Streams, and Events
system-design.description: Decouple parts of a system with messages. You will use queues for background work, streams for ordered event logs, and patterns that keep processing correct when messages repeat or arrive late.
topics: Kafka partitions, offsets and consumer groups
Dead-letter queues and retries with backoff
Event sourcing and the outbox pattern
system-design.challenge: Design an order-processing pipeline with a queue between checkout and fulfillment: make consumers idempotent, add retries with exponential backoff and a dead-letter queue, and describe how the outbox pattern guarantees an order is never saved without its event.

children.title: Queues, pub/sub and logs
children.description: A queue gives each message to one worker; pub/sub gives it to every subscriber; a log keeps ordered history that consumers can replay.

children.title: Delivery guarantees
children.description: Networks fail, so exactly-once is hard. Most systems deliver at least once and make consumers safe to repeat.

children.title: Idempotent consumers
children.description: Track processed message ids or make operations naturally repeatable so a redelivered message has no extra effect.

children.title: Retries and dead letters
children.description: Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, and move poison messages to a dead-letter queue for inspection.

resources.label: AWS Builders' Library - Timeouts, retries and backoff

children.title: Topics, partitions and offsets
children.description: A topic is split into partitions; order is guaranteed only within one. Consumers track their position by offset.

children.title: Consumer groups
children.description: Consumers in a group share partitions so work scales out. Adding more consumers than partitions gains nothing.

children.title: The outbox pattern
children.description: Write the business change and the event in one database transaction, then publish from the outbox. It avoids saving data without its event.

children.title: Event sourcing
children.description: Store the sequence of events as the source of truth and derive current state from it. It gives history and replay at the cost of complexity.

system-design.title: Consistency, CAP, and Distributed Coordination
system-design.description: Understand what you can and cannot promise when machines and networks fail. You will use CAP and consistency models to reason about trade-offs, learn how consensus works, and know when to use coordination services.
topics: CAP theorem and what it really says
Clocks, ordering and the problem with time
system-design.challenge: Take three systems you use (a bank transfer, a social feed and a shopping cart) and for each choose a consistency model, justify it against CAP, and describe what a user observes during a network partition.

children.title: CAP theorem
children.description: During a network partition a system must choose between consistency and availability. The theorem is about that moment, not normal operation.

children.title: Consistency models
children.description: Linearizable, sequential, causal and eventual consistency promise different things. Stronger models are easier to use and more expensive.

children.title: Read and write quorums
children.description: With N replicas, requiring W writes and R reads where W + R > N makes reads see the latest write. Tuning W and R trades latency for safety.

children.title: Conflict resolution
children.description: Concurrent writes need a rule: last write wins, version vectors or CRDTs. Each loses or merges data differently.

children.title: Raft
children.description: Raft elects a leader, replicates a log to a majority and applies entries in order. It is designed to be understandable.

children.title: Coordination services
children.description: ZooKeeper, etcd and Consul give you consensus as a service for leader election, configuration and locks, so you do not build it yourself.

children.title: Clocks cannot be trusted
children.description: Machine clocks drift and differ, so you cannot order events across servers by timestamp alone. Logical clocks and versions are safer.

children.title: Distributed locks and leases
children.description: A lock holder can pause and lose the lock without knowing. Fencing tokens make stale holders harmless.

resources.label: Martin Kleppmann - How to do distributed locking

system-design.title: Microservices and Service Communication
system-design.description: Decide when to split a system and how services should talk. You will compare monoliths and microservices honestly, manage data across services with sagas, and use gateways, discovery and meshes.
topics: Distributed transactions and the saga pattern
system-design.challenge: Split an e-commerce monolith on paper: draw the service boundaries, decide which calls are synchronous and which events, design the order saga with compensations for payment failure, and list what you would keep in the monolith and why.

children.title: Monolith versus microservices
children.description: Microservices buy independent deployment at the price of network failures and operational overhead. A modular monolith is often the better start.

children.title: Finding service boundaries
children.description: Split along business capabilities, where data and change rate differ, not along technical layers.

children.title: Database per service
children.description: Each service owns its data and exposes it through an API, which avoids hidden coupling through a shared schema.

children.title: Sagas
children.description: A saga replaces a distributed transaction with local steps and compensating actions that undo earlier steps when a later one fails.

children.title: Synchronous versus events
children.description: Synchronous calls are simple but chain failures together; events decouple services but make flows harder to follow.

children.title: Gateways and discovery
children.description: A gateway gives clients one entry point, and discovery lets services find each other as instances come and go.

children.title: Service meshes
children.description: A mesh moves retries, timeouts, mutual TLS and telemetry into sidecars. It helps at scale and adds complexity before you need it.

children.title: Contracts and compatibility
children.description: Add fields, do not remove or repurpose them, and test consumers against provider contracts so services can deploy independently.

system-design.title: Reliability: Rate Limiting, Resilience, and Failure
system-design.description: Design for the failures that will happen. You will limit load, isolate failures with timeouts, retries and circuit breakers, degrade gracefully, and test your assumptions with controlled failure.
topics: Rate limiting algorithms and where to apply them
Timeouts, retries and exponential backoff with jitter
system-design.challenge: Add resilience to a checkout service that depends on payment, inventory and email: set timeouts and a retry budget, put a circuit breaker on the payment call, define a degraded mode when email is down, and write a failure drill that removes each dependency in turn.

children.title: Rate limiting algorithms
children.description: Token bucket and sliding window limit how fast a client can call you. They protect shared resources and enforce fairness.

resources.label: Stripe - Scaling your API with rate limiters

children.title: Load shedding
children.description: When overloaded, reject low-priority work early so important requests still succeed, instead of failing everything slowly.

children.title: Timeouts and retries
children.description: Every network call needs a timeout. Retries multiply load during an outage unless they use backoff, jitter and a budget.

resources.label: AWS Builders' Library - Timeouts, retries and backoff

children.title: Circuit breakers and bulkheads
children.description: A circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency, and bulkheads keep one slow dependency from using all your threads.

children.title: Redundancy and failover
children.description: No single points of failure means duplicating each component and testing the switch. Untested failover usually fails.

children.title: Multi-region design
children.description: Multiple regions survive a regional outage but force hard choices about data replication and consistency.

children.title: Degrading features
children.description: Decide in advance which features can fail without taking the product down, such as recommendations or email, and serve a simpler version.

children.title: Chaos engineering
children.description: Deliberately injecting failures in a controlled way finds weaknesses before real incidents do.

system-design.title: Observability, Capacity, and Cost
system-design.description: Operate what you design. You will instrument systems with metrics, logs and traces, define alerts that matter, plan capacity from data and keep cost in view as a design constraint.
topics: The four golden signals and RED/USE methods
Alerting on symptoms and SLO burn rate
system-design.challenge: Instrument a small multi-service app with OpenTelemetry, build a dashboard with the four golden signals, define an SLO and a burn-rate alert, run a load test to find the first bottleneck and estimate the monthly cloud cost at 10x traffic.

children.title: Metrics, logs and traces
children.description: Metrics show trends, logs explain single events and traces follow one request across services. You need all three.

children.title: Golden signals
children.description: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation tell you whether a service is healthy. Start dashboards with these four.

resources.label: Google SRE Book - Monitoring distributed systems

children.title: Distributed tracing
children.description: A trace id passed through every call shows where time is spent in a request that touches many services.

children.title: Structured logging
children.description: Log events as structured fields with request ids, so you can search and correlate them instead of grepping text.

children.title: Alert on symptoms
children.description: Page people for user-visible problems, not for every internal metric. Too many alerts cause alert fatigue.

children.title: SLO burn rate
children.description: Alerting on how fast the error budget is being used catches both sudden outages and slow degradation.

resources.label: Google SRE Workbook - Alerting on SLOs

children.title: Capacity planning
children.description: Load test to find limits, measure growth, and add headroom. Autoscaling reacts to load but not instantly.

resources.label: Google SRE Book - Software engineering in SRE

children.title: Designing for cost
children.description: Data transfer, storage tiers and idle capacity dominate cloud bills. Estimate cost during design, not after the invoice.

system-design.title: Classic System Designs I: Storage, Feeds, and Identifiers
system-design.description: Apply everything to well-known problems. You will design a URL shortener, a distributed ID generator, a rate limiter and a news feed, practicing the full cycle of requirements, estimation, design and trade-offs.
topics: URL shortener and ID generation (Snowflake style)
News feed: fan-out on write versus read
system-design.challenge: Write complete designs for a URL shortener and a news feed: requirements, capacity estimates, API, data model, high-level diagram, a deep dive on the hardest component, and a bottleneck review. Present one aloud in 35 minutes.

children.title: Generating short keys
children.description: Base62 of a counter, a hash with collision handling and a pre-generated key service each trade simplicity, predictability and coordination.

children.title: Read-heavy scaling
children.description: Redirects are read thousands of times per write, so cache aggressively and keep the database off the hot path.

children.title: Distributed ID generation
children.description: Snowflake-style ids combine a timestamp, machine id and sequence to give unique, roughly ordered ids without coordination.

children.title: Object storage
children.description: Large files go to object storage with metadata in a database; clients upload directly using signed URLs.

children.title: Fan-out on write versus read
children.description: Precomputing feeds at write time makes reads fast but costs a lot for accounts with millions of followers. Many systems mix both.

children.title: Ranking and the celebrity problem
children.description: A hybrid approach handles celebrities differently from normal users so one post does not trigger millions of writes.

children.title: Notification system
children.description: Notifications flow through queues to per-channel workers, with templates, preferences, deduplication and retries.

children.title: Reviewing for bottlenecks
children.description: After the first design, trace a request and ask what breaks at ten times the load. Name the weakest point and fix it.

system-design.title: Classic System Designs II: Chat, Media, Search, and Payments
system-design.description: Tackle the harder classics: real-time messaging, video delivery, search and money movement. These designs combine persistent connections, large objects, indexes and strict correctness.
topics: Chat system: WebSockets, presence, ordering and delivery
Video streaming: upload, transcoding, adaptive bitrate, CDN
Search: inverted indexes, ranking and typeahead
Presenting a design and handling follow-ups
system-design.challenge: Design a chat app supporting 1:1 and group messages and a payment flow for a marketplace. For each, specify guarantees (ordering, delivery, exactly-once effects), failure scenarios and recovery, then practice presenting one end to end including follow-up questions.

children.title: Persistent connections
children.description: WebSockets keep a connection open for pushes. Servers need a way to find which node holds a user's connection to route messages.

children.title: Ordering and delivery
children.description: Per-conversation sequence numbers give ordering, acknowledgements give delivery, and offline users get messages from storage on reconnect.

children.title: Video pipeline
children.description: Uploads are split, transcoded into several resolutions and served in adaptive-bitrate chunks from a CDN.

children.title: Large file handling
children.description: Resumable uploads, chunking and direct-to-storage transfers keep big files off your application servers.

children.title: Inverted indexes
children.description: A search index maps each term to the documents containing it, which makes lookup fast. Ranking then scores the candidates.

children.title: Typeahead
children.description: Autocomplete uses a trie or prefix index with popularity data, cached close to users because it runs on every keystroke.

children.title: Idempotent payments and ledgers
children.description: Money systems need idempotent requests and an append-only ledger so every cent is traceable and double charges are impossible.

children.title: Reconciliation
children.description: Periodically compare your records with the payment provider's to catch missed or duplicated events. Assume your own system can be wrong.

software-design.title: Clean Code and Code Smells
software-design.description: Learn to write code that the next person can read. You will name things well, keep functions small and single-purpose, and spot the smells that signal a design problem.
topics: Small functions and a single level of abstraction
Comments: when they help and when they hide a smell
Common smells: long method, large class, duplication
software-design.challenge: Take a 150-line function from your own code and rewrite it for readability. List each smell you removed and why.

children.title: Intent-revealing names
children.description: A name should say why something exists and how it is used. If you need a comment to explain a variable, rename it instead.

children.title: Small functions, one level of abstraction
children.description: A function should do one thing at one level of detail. Extract the steps so the top-level function reads like an outline.

children.title: When a comment helps
children.description: Good comments record why a decision was made, a trap, or a constraint the code cannot show. Comments that repeat the code only go stale.

children.title: Linters and team conventions
children.description: Let tools settle style arguments. A formatter and linter in CI keep diffs about behavior, not whitespace.

children.title: Long method and large class
children.description: Size is a symptom: the unit is doing several jobs. Split along responsibilities and name each piece for what it does.

children.title: Duplication
children.description: Copied logic must be fixed in every copy. Extract it once the third copy appears, and only when the copies truly mean the same thing.

children.title: Errors without noise
children.description: Handle failures at the level that can do something about them. Scattered try/catch blocks and silent returns hide the real flow.

children.title: Consistent error strategy
children.description: Pick one style per codebase (exceptions, result values) and use it everywhere, so callers know what to expect.

software-design.title: Object-Oriented Design Done Right
software-design.description: Use objects to model behavior, not just to hold data. You will practice encapsulation, favor composition over inheritance, and decide when polymorphism earns its keep.
topics: Tell, do not ask; the Law of Demeter

resources.label: Head First Object-Oriented Analysis and Design

software-design.challenge: Model a library system with inheritance, then redo it with composition. Write down which version is easier to change.

children.title: Hiding internal state
children.description: Keep fields private and expose behavior. Callers then depend on what an object does, so you can change how it works.

resources.label: Head First Object-Oriented Analysis and Design

children.title: Tell, do not ask
children.description: Instead of pulling data out to make a decision, tell the object what to do. Logic ends up next to the data it uses.

children.title: Why inheritance is fragile
children.description: A subclass is tied to its parent's internals, so a change in the base can break every child. Use inheritance only for a true is-a relationship.

resources.label: Head First Object-Oriented Analysis and Design

children.title: Composition over inheritance
children.description: Build behavior by combining small objects you can swap at runtime, instead of fixing it in a class tree.

children.title: Polymorphism and interfaces
children.description: Code against what an object can do, not its concrete class. A new implementation then plugs in without touching the callers.

children.title: Replacing type checks
children.description: A chain of if or switch on a type tag is a hint to push the behavior into each type instead.

resources.label: Refactoring Guru - Replace Conditional with Polymorphism

children.title: Cohesion
children.description: A cohesive class has parts that belong together. If you cannot name it without "and", it probably does two jobs.

children.title: Coupling and the Law of Demeter
children.description: A method should talk to its direct collaborators, not reach through a chain of objects. Long chains spread knowledge across the code.

software-design.title: SOLID Principles
software-design.description: Apply the five SOLID principles through before-and-after refactors. For each one you will see the problem it solves and the cost of overdoing it.

resources.label: Agile Software Development, Principles, Patterns, and Practices

software-design.challenge: Find one class in a real project that breaks two SOLID principles. Refactor it and explain each change in a short write-up.

children.title: Single responsibility
children.description: A module should have one reason to change. Group code by who asks for changes, not by technical layer.

children.title: Open for extension, closed for modification
children.description: Add behavior by adding new code, not by editing tested code. Abstractions and strategies are the usual way to get there.

children.title: Liskov substitution
children.description: Any subtype must work wherever its parent is expected. A subclass that throws on an inherited method breaks that promise.

resources.label: Head First Object-Oriented Analysis and Design

children.title: Interface segregation
children.description: Many small, focused interfaces beat one large one. Clients should not depend on methods they never call.

children.title: Depending on abstractions
children.description: High-level policy should not import low-level details. Both depend on an interface owned by the high-level side.

children.title: Dependency injection
children.description: Pass collaborators in instead of creating them inside. That makes code configurable and lets tests supply fakes.

resources.label: Martin Fowler - Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern

children.title: When SOLID is over-engineering
children.description: An interface with one implementation and a factory for a constant adds cost without benefit. Apply a principle when change actually hurts.

children.title: Spotting violations in real code
children.description: A class that needs edits for every new feature, or tests that need heavy setup, usually breaks one of the principles.

software-design.title: Creational Patterns
software-design.description: Control how objects get created. You will use factories, builders and dependency injection, and learn why the singleton is usually a trap.
topics: Singleton and why it hurts testing
Dependency injection as a modern replacement
Choosing a pattern versus a plain function
software-design.challenge: Build a notification sender that creates email, SMS and push senders through a factory. Add a new channel without editing existing code.

children.title: Factory method
children.description: Let a method decide which class to create, so callers depend on a product interface and not a concrete type.

children.title: Abstract factory
children.description: Create whole families of related objects, such as one UI theme's widgets, behind one interface.

children.title: Builder for complex construction
children.description: Build an object step by step when it has many optional parts. It replaces long constructors with readable, named calls.

children.title: Builders in practice
children.description: Fluent query builders and request configurators are everyday examples. Validate the result when you call build.

children.title: Singleton and why it hurts testing
children.description: A global instance hides dependencies and leaks state between tests. Prefer passing one shared object in.

children.title: Object pools and prototypes
children.description: Reuse expensive objects or clone a ready-made one instead of building from scratch. Measure before you add the complexity.

children.title: Dependency injection as a replacement
children.description: A container or plain constructor arguments often remove the need for factories and singletons.

resources.label: Martin Fowler - Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern

children.title: A pattern or a plain function
children.description: In many languages a function or an object literal does the job. Use a pattern when it removes real duplication or coupling.

software-design.title: Structural Patterns
software-design.description: Combine objects into larger structures without tangling them. You will wrap third-party code with adapters, add behavior with decorators and hide complexity behind facades.
topics: Facade for a simple entry point
Proxy for access control and lazy loading
software-design.challenge: Wrap two different payment providers behind one interface with adapters, then add logging with a decorator.

children.title: Adapter for third-party APIs
children.description: Wrap an outside API in your own interface so a vendor change touches one file, not the whole codebase.

children.title: Facade
children.description: Give a messy subsystem one simple entry point. Callers use the facade, and the details can change behind it.

children.title: Decorator for stacking behavior
children.description: Wrap an object with another that has the same interface to add logging, caching or retries without subclassing.

children.title: Proxy for access and lazy loading
children.description: A stand-in controls access to the real object. Use it for permission checks, lazy loading and caching.

children.title: Composite for tree structures
children.description: Treat a single item and a group of items the same way. File systems and UI component trees follow this shape.

children.title: Walking a composite
children.description: Operations such as size or render recurse over children. Keep the child list behind the composite's interface.

children.title: Middleware as a chain
children.description: Express middleware wraps each request with small steps. That is the decorator and chain ideas in daily use.

children.title: Choosing among structural patterns
children.description: Adapter changes an interface, facade simplifies one, decorator adds behavior and proxy controls access. Name the problem first.

software-design.title: Behavioral Patterns
software-design.description: Organize how objects talk and make decisions. You will replace long conditionals with strategies and states, and decouple components with observers and commands.
topics: Command, undo and queues of actions
Template method and chain of responsibility
Spotting patterns in frameworks you already use
software-design.challenge: Implement a vending machine as a state machine, then a pricing engine with swappable discount strategies.

children.title: Strategy to swap algorithms
children.description: Put each algorithm behind a common interface and choose one at runtime. It replaces large conditionals.

children.title: Template method
children.description: A base class fixes the steps of a process and lets subclasses fill in some of them. Prefer strategy when you can.

children.title: Observer and event-driven design
children.description: A subject notifies subscribers without knowing who they are. Event emitters and UI listeners work this way.

children.title: Observer pitfalls
children.description: Forgotten unsubscribes leak memory, and long event chains are hard to trace. Keep handlers small and name events clearly.

children.title: Command, undo and queues
children.description: Turn a request into an object so you can queue it, log it, retry it or undo it.

children.title: State machines
children.description: Model behavior that changes with state as explicit states and transitions, not flags scattered in conditionals.

children.title: Chain of responsibility
children.description: Pass a request along a list of handlers until one deals with it. Auth, validation and error handling pipelines use it.

children.title: Patterns inside frameworks
children.description: Reducers, hooks, middleware and plugins are patterns with new names. Recognizing them speeds up learning a new framework.

software-design.title: Refactoring Safely
software-design.description: Change structure without changing behavior. You will write tests around code you do not trust, then improve it in small, reversible steps.
topics: Small steps and the refactoring catalog
software-design.challenge: Pick an untested module, add characterization tests, then refactor it in at least five small commits with passing tests each time.

children.title: Characterization tests
children.description: Before changing legacy code, write tests that pin down what it does today, right or wrong. They tell you if a change altered behavior.

children.title: Seams for testing
children.description: Find or create a place where you can swap a dependency without editing the code under test. Then you can test the untested.

children.title: The refactoring catalog
children.description: Named, small transformations with known safe steps. Work from the catalog and run tests after each one.

children.title: Extract, move and rename
children.description: These three moves do most of the work. Extract a function, move it to the class that owns the data, then rename for clarity.

children.title: Replace conditionals with polymorphism
children.description: When a type switch repeats across the code, move each branch into its own class behind one interface.

resources.label: Refactoring Guru - Replace Conditional with Polymorphism

children.title: Strangler pattern for rewrites
children.description: Build the new system around the old one and move traffic over piece by piece. You never need a risky big-bang switch.

children.title: Measuring a refactor
children.description: Check that tests still pass, that the change is smaller or clearer, and that the next feature is easier. A refactor with no payoff is churn.

children.title: Refactoring in a team
children.description: Keep refactoring commits separate from feature commits and review them on their own. Small, frequent changes are easier to reverse.

software-design.title: Layered, Hexagonal, and Clean Architecture
software-design.description: Structure a whole application so business rules do not depend on frameworks or databases. You will compare layered, hexagonal and clean architecture and apply the dependency rule.
topics: Keeping the domain free of framework code

resources.label: Get Your Hands Dirty on Clean Architecture

software-design.challenge: Restructure a small Express app into controller, service and repository layers, with the database swappable behind an interface.

children.title: Layered architecture and its leaks
children.description: Presentation, domain and data layers keep concerns apart. Layers leak when SQL or HTTP details climb into the domain.

children.title: Controllers, services and repositories
children.description: Controllers translate HTTP, services hold the rules and repositories hide storage. Each calls only the layer below.

children.title: Ports and adapters
children.description: The core defines ports, the interfaces it needs. Adapters for databases, queues and web plug into them from outside.

resources.label: Netflix - Ready for changes with Hexagonal Architecture

children.title: Swapping adapters
children.description: Because the core never imports an adapter, you can replace a database or add a CLI without rewriting business rules.

children.title: Dependencies point inward
children.description: Source code in outer rings may know about inner rings, never the reverse. The domain imports nothing from the framework.

children.title: Domain free of framework code
children.description: Keep entities as plain classes. Annotations and ORM types belong in adapters, where they cannot spread.

children.title: Unit tests for the core
children.description: Domain logic with no I/O needs no mocks and runs in milliseconds. Put most of your tests here.

children.title: Integration tests for adapters
children.description: Test each adapter against the real thing, such as a database container, and keep those tests few and focused.

software-design.title: Domain-Driven Design Essentials
software-design.description: Model the business first. You will separate entities from value objects, draw aggregate boundaries and split a system into bounded contexts with a shared language.
software-design.challenge: Model an online store with aggregates and bounded contexts for orders, catalog and billing. Draw the context map and justify each boundary.

children.title: Ubiquitous language
children.description: Use the same words in conversation, documents and code. If the business says "policy", the class is not called "Contract".

children.title: Modeling with domain experts
children.description: Sketch the model together, listen for words that mean different things, and rename in code when understanding changes.

children.title: Entities and value objects
children.description: An entity has an identity that persists. A value object is defined by its values and is immutable, such as money or a date range.

children.title: Aggregates and consistency
children.description: An aggregate is a cluster that changes together under one root. Keep transactions inside one aggregate.

children.title: Domain events
children.description: Record that something important happened, such as OrderPlaced, and let other parts react without being called directly.

children.title: Bounded contexts
children.description: A word can mean different things in different parts of a business. Give each meaning its own context and model.

children.title: Context maps and translation
children.description: Show how contexts relate and translate between them at the border. An anti-corruption layer stops a legacy model from leaking in.

children.title: When DDD is too heavy
children.description: A simple CRUD app does not need aggregates and events. Use the full approach only where the domain is complex and changing.

software-design.title: Modules, Monoliths, and Service Boundaries
software-design.description: Decide where code boundaries belong. You will build a modular monolith, enforce module boundaries and learn when splitting into services is worth the cost.
software-design.challenge: Map the modules in a project you know, draw the dependency graph, and fix one boundary violation.

children.title: Structuring a modular monolith
children.description: One deployable, split into modules with clear owners. You get most of the benefit of services without the network.

children.title: Public interfaces between modules
children.description: Each module exposes a small API and hides the rest. Other modules never reach into its tables or classes.

children.title: Direction of dependencies
children.description: Draw the module graph and keep it acyclic. A cycle means two modules are really one.

children.title: Detecting hidden coupling
children.description: Shared tables, shared constants and changes that always happen together reveal coupling the imports do not show.

children.title: Shared libraries versus duplication
children.description: A shared library couples every user to its release. Duplicating a small piece is sometimes cheaper than a shared dependency.

children.title: Moving from monolith to services
children.description: Extract a service when a boundary is stable and a team or scaling need justifies the cost of a network call.

children.title: Conway's law
children.description: A system's design mirrors the communication of the teams that build it. Shape teams to match the architecture you want.

children.title: Team-aligned boundaries
children.description: Give each team ownership of a whole module so it can ship without coordinating every change.

software-design.title: API and Interface Design
software-design.description: Design the seams other code depends on. You will define clear contracts, handle errors consistently and change an interface without breaking its users.
topics: Error handling strategy across a codebase
software-design.challenge: Design the public interface of a small library, write usage examples first, then evolve it with one breaking and one non-breaking change.

children.title: Small, deep interfaces
children.description: A good interface is simple to use and hides a lot of work. Wide interfaces with shallow behavior make users learn more than they gain.

children.title: Naming and consistency
children.description: Use the same name and shape for the same idea across the API, so a user can guess correctly.

children.title: Validation at the boundary
children.description: Check and parse input once where it enters, then pass trusted types inward. Do not re-check in every function.

children.title: Error handling strategy
children.description: Return errors that say what happened and what the caller can do. Keep error shapes the same across the whole API.

children.title: Backward-compatible changes
children.description: Adding an optional field is safe. Removing or renaming one breaks callers, so treat it as a new version.

children.title: Versioning
children.description: Version when you must break compatibility, give users a clear deprecation window, and avoid running too many versions at once.

children.title: Idempotency
children.description: A repeated request should have the same effect as one. Idempotency keys make retries safe for payments and orders.

children.title: Documenting the contract
children.description: Write the contract in a machine-readable spec and keep it in sync with the code through tests or generation.

software-design.title: Low-Level Design Interview Problems
software-design.description: Turn everything into interview practice. You will clarify requirements, pick classes and relationships, apply patterns where they fit and code a clean solution under time pressure.
topics: A framework for low-level design rounds
LRU cache and rate limiter classes
Presenting trade-offs and extending the design

resources.label: Grokking the Low Level Design Interview

software-design.challenge: Solve three problems (parking lot, LRU cache, elevator) in 45 minutes each: class diagram, core code and one extension per problem.

children.title: A framework for LLD rounds
children.description: Clarify requirements, list entities, define relationships, sketch the main classes and methods, then walk through a scenario.

resources.label: Grokking the Low Level Design Interview

children.title: Choosing patterns on purpose
children.description: Name the variation you expect, such as pricing rules, and use a pattern for that point only. Say why out loud.

children.title: Parking lot and elevator
children.description: Practice modeling spaces, vehicles and requests. The elevator adds a scheduling strategy and a state machine.

children.title: LRU cache and rate limiter
children.description: Both combine a data structure with a policy. Make the eviction or limiting policy swappable.

children.title: Chess and tic-tac-toe
children.description: Model the board, pieces and rules separately. Keep move validation out of the piece classes if rules grow.

children.title: Booking and inventory
children.description: Think about concurrent requests and double booking. Model holds, confirmations and expirations explicitly.

children.title: Explaining trade-offs
children.description: State what you chose, what you gave up and when you would choose differently. That is what the interviewer is listening for.
